title: Kwete
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Grain soaked a day or two, germinated two to three days, sun-dried two, soured in a sealed container, roasted, mashed, fermented and strained through cloth — finished when it is cream to light brown with a thick, consistent sweet-sour taste.
longDesc: Kwete is the Lugbara beer of West Nile, brewed from sorghum raised with a yeast they call aku fi, and it is drunk after eating because it is believed to aid digestion and keep the stomach healthy. The doneness cue is one of the clearest in Ugandan brewing and it is both visual and tasted: high-quality kwete is cream to light brown in colour with a thick, consistent sweet-sour taste. The final straining through cloth is what gives it that uniform appearance.
ingredients: Fermented sorghum — or millet, or maize
// No ratios and no beverage-stage duration are documented for this version
steps: Sour the grain in a sealed container.
Add the yeast, aku fi, and let it ferment.
Strain through cloth for a uniform appearance.
It is right when it is cream to light brown in colour with a thick, consistent sweet-sour taste.
Serve in calabashes, after a meal.
chefTips: Cream to light brown, thick, and a consistent sweet-sour taste. That is the documented quality standard and it covers colour, body and flavour at once.
Strain it through cloth. That is what produces the uniform appearance the standard describes, and an unstrained brew will not look right however well it ferments.

The name kwete covers at least two different drinks in Uganda and they should not be merged. This is the Lugbara sorghum one, raised with aku fi. The Kampala maize version, UGA088, has a separate and much larger research literature and is a different drink.
No ratios exist for this version, and no duration for the beverage-stage fermentation. The grain stages are documented; the brewing is not.
Traditionally drunk after eating, and believed to aid digestion and maintain stomach health. That is the Lugbara framing for it.
West Nile markets serve it in calabashes called icereke. It is now produced nationwide, Kampala included.

The Lugbara attribution in the most accessible source is uncited, which is worth knowing. The process details come from a 1974 Makerere Institute of Social Research study, which does carry a citation.
The same name is used for related beverages by the Abanyala ba Kakamega in Kenya, in DR Congo, by the Pojulu of South Sudan and the Bukusu of Kenya.
commonMistakes: Skipping the souring stage in the sealed container.
Confusing it with the Kampala maize kwete.
Drinking it before a meal rather than after, which is not how it is used.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on kwete, whose process detail is cited to Christine C. Wallace and Sheldon G. Weeks, 'Success Or Failure in Rural Uganda: A Study of Young People', Makerere Institute of Social Research, Makerere University, 1974, p83 — the 24-to-48-hour soak, 48-to-72-hour germination, roughly 48-hour sun-drying, souring in a sealed container, roasting, mashing, fermenting and straining through cloth, the ingredients including the yeast locally termed aku fi, and the quality standard that high-quality kwete is cream to light brown in colour with a thick, consistent sweet-sour taste are all from that source.

The attribution to the Lugbara, the use of sorghum fermented by aku fi, and the custom of drinking it after eating to aid digestion and maintain stomach health are from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which gives no citations for these points. That is stated rather than hidden.
The icereke calabashes of West Nile markets, and the drink's spread to Kampala and to communities in Kenya, DR Congo and South Sudan, are from the kwete article.
No ratios and no beverage-stage fermentation duration are documented for this version in any source consulted.
healthBenefits: Sorghum is high in fibre, iron and B vitamins and is naturally gluten-free.
Lactic and yeast fermentation together raise mineral availability.
Traditionally taken for digestion, which is the community's own framing.
An alcoholic drink of undocumented strength.
culturalNote: That kwete is drunk after eating rather than before, and specifically for the stomach, is a small detail that says a lot — it belongs to the meal rather than to the evening. West Nile is the least documented food region in Uganda and this is one of the few things from it that has a written quality standard at all.
